title: 22. Interview: RAG Evaluation Techniques
summary: Interview Q&A for RAG Evaluation Techniques.
objectives: Answer the RAG Evaluation Techniques interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: PRECISION@K — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
sections.body:
### 🧠 10 Conceptual Questions

| #   | Question                                                                                | Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **What does Precision@K measure and why is "K" important?**                             | Precision@K measures what fraction of the top-K retrieved documents are relevant. K defines the cutoff point — in real systems, users typically only look at the first K results. A high K could dilute precision if irrelevant docs are added. |
| 2   | **Why can Precision@K be misleading when used alone?**                                  | A system retrieving only 1 highly relevant doc would have Precision@1 = 1.0, but may miss many other relevant docs. Precision alone ignores recall — you need both to evaluate a retriever fairly.                                              |
| 3   | **How does Precision@K differ from standard precision in binary classification?**       | Standard precision evaluates over ALL predictions. Precision@K only evaluates the TOP K retrieved results, regardless of how many total documents exist. It's positional — the ordering matters.                                                |
| 4   | **What is the relationship between Precision@K and Recall@K as K increases?**           | As K increases, Recall@K generally increases (you retrieve more relevant docs) while Precision@K often decreases (more irrelevant docs added to hit). There's an inverse tradeoff.                                                              |
| 5   | **In RAG systems, why do we typically use small K values (3-5) for Precision@K?**       | In RAG, you pass retrieved chunks to an LLM. Using too many chunks increases token cost, noise in context, and hallucination risk. K=3-5 is practical for LLM context windows.                                                                  |
| 6   | **How would you interpret Precision@5 = 0.40 for a medical RAG system?**                | Only 2 out of 5 retrieved documents are relevant. In a medical system, this is dangerous — the LLM generator receives 3 irrelevant chunks that could confuse or mislead the answer. This requires immediate improvement.                        |
| 7   | **What is the difference between mean Precision@K and Precision@K for a single query?** | Single-query P@K evaluates one search request. Mean P@K (MAP@K) averages across many queries, giving a holistic view of the retriever's performance across diverse inputs.                                                                      |
| 8   | **Can Precision@K be 1.0 while Recall@K is very low? Give an example.**                 | Yes. If only 1 document is retrieved (K=1) and it's relevant, Precision@1 = 1.0. But if 10 relevant docs exist, Recall@1 = 0.10. This shows precision and recall must be evaluated together.                                                    |
| 9   | **How does Precision@K relate to context precision in RAG evaluation?**                 | Context Precision directly inherits the concept from Precision@K — it measures how many of the retrieved context chunks are actually useful for generating the correct answer, instead of just measuring topical relevance.                     |
| 10  | **Why is Precision@K not a good metric for long-tail query distributions?**             | For rare queries, ground truth labels are sparse. A retriever might achieve high P@K by chance on common queries but fail on tail queries. Averaging across query types hides this performance gap.                                             |

### 🎭 10 Scenario-Based Questions

| #   | Scenario                                                                                                                | Question & Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1   | **Medical chatbot retrieving K=5 documents for "Diabetes type 2 diet". Only 2 are relevant.**                           | **Q:** What is Precision@5 and what action should you take? **A:** P@5 = 2/5 = 0.40. This is dangerously low for medical. Actions: improve embedding model, add query expansion, use reranker like CohereRerank to filter top-K results.                                             |
| 2   | **E-commerce returns 10 products for "running shoes". 8 are truly running shoes.**                                      | **Q:** What is Precision@10 and what does it mean for UX? **A:** P@10 = 0.80. Good precision — 80% of shown products are relevant. Users likely satisfied. Could still improve by removing the 2 irrelevant results.                                                                 |
| 3   | **Legal RAG system: retrieved K=5 case laws, 3 relevant. After adding a reranker, 4 become relevant.**                  | **Q:** Calculate improvement and explain why reranker helped. **A:** P@5 improved from 3/5=0.60 to 4/5=0.80 (+33%). Reranker reorders retrieved docs using cross-encoder that computes query-document interaction jointly, improving relevance ranking.                              |
| 4   | **You're evaluating two RAG systems: System A has P@3=0.9, System B has P@10=0.9.**                                     | **Q:** Which system is better and why? **A:** System A is better for RAG use cases. High precision at K=3 means top retrieved chunks are almost always relevant, minimizing noise fed to LLM. System B needs 10 docs to achieve same precision.                                      |
| 5   | **Your retriever Precision@5 = 0.60 but the end-to-end RAG answer quality is still poor.**                              | **Q:** What could explain this disconnect? **A:** Even 60% precision might cause the LLM to get confused by 2 irrelevant chunks. Also, faithfulness, answer relevancy, or insufficient context recall could be failing. Retrieval precision alone doesn't guarantee good generation. |
| 6   | **Customer support RAG: Precision@K drops from 0.80 to 0.50 when you increase K from 3 to 10.**                         | **Q:** Should you use K=3 or K=10? **A:** K=3 for most queries (higher precision, less noise). K=10 only for complex queries where recall is critical. Implement adaptive K based on query complexity score.                                                                         |
| 7   | **You add 50,000 new documents to your knowledge base. Precision@5 drops from 0.75 to 0.55.**                           | **Q:** Why might this happen and how would you fix it? **A:** New documents may be lower quality, overlapping, or create false neighbors in embedding space. Fix: clean and deduplicate new docs, increase embedding model dimensionality, add metadata filters.                     |
| 8   | **RAG for code search: "Python async function examples" retrieves 5 docs. 3 are Python async, 2 are JavaScript async.** | **Q:** Precision@5 = 0.60. How would you specifically improve it? **A:** Add language metadata filter. Use hybrid search (BM25 + semantic). Include "programming language:Python" constraint in retrieval query. Fine-tune embedding model on code data.                             |
| 9   | **Finance RAG: P@5 for Q1 reports = 0.85, but for complex multi-document queries = 0.40.**                              | **Q:** How would you address the complex query problem? **A:** Implement query decomposition — break complex queries into sub-queries, retrieve for each, then combine. Use HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embedding) or step-back prompting.                                           |
| 10  | **You observe P@K is high in offline evaluation but users report bad answers in production.**                           | **Q:** What could cause this train/test distribution mismatch? **A:** Offline evaluation uses curated queries; production has messy, ambiguous queries. Ground truth labels may be stale. Solution: continuously sample and label production queries for evaluation.                 |

sections.title: RECALL@K — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
sections.body:
### 🧠 10 Conceptual Questions

| #   | Question                                                                                        | Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1   | **What does Recall@K measure in the context of information retrieval?**                         | Recall@K measures what fraction of ALL relevant documents in the knowledge base were successfully retrieved in the top-K results. It answers: "Did the retriever find everything that exists?"                                                                           |
| 2   | **Why is Recall@K especially critical for RAG in medical or legal domains?**                    | Missing a relevant document (low recall) could mean the LLM cannot mention a critical drug interaction or legal precedent. Incomplete information = incomplete answer. In high-stakes domains, missing info can be dangerous.                                            |
| 3   | **Explain the fundamental tension between Precision@K and Recall@K.**                           | To increase recall, you retrieve more documents (increase K), but this dilutes precision with irrelevant docs. Conversely, high precision with small K means you'll miss many relevant docs. It's impossible to simultaneously maximize both without a better retriever. |
| 4   | **How would you calculate Recall@K if the total number of relevant documents is unknown?**      | You need an annotated dataset where all relevant docs are labeled for each query. Without ground truth, you can approximate using LLM-as-Judge to score each retrieved doc, and sample a random set of non-retrieved docs to estimate missed relevant ones.              |
| 5   | **What is the difference between Recall@K and Context Recall in RAGAS?**                        | Recall@K measures what fraction of ALL relevant docs in the KB were retrieved. Context Recall measures what fraction of information needed to answer the question was present in the retrieved context. Context Recall is more answer-oriented.                          |
| 6   | **How does chunking strategy affect Recall@K in RAG systems?**                                  | Smaller chunks → more chunks → higher chance of retrieving at least one relevant chunk (higher recall) but each chunk has less context. Larger chunks → fewer chunks → may miss some relevant passages. Chunk size is a key tuning parameter for recall.                 |
| 7   | **What is "semantic recall" and how does it differ from standard Recall@K?**                    | Standard Recall@K relies on exact relevant document IDs. Semantic recall uses embedding similarity to estimate coverage — a retrieved chunk that semantically covers the same information as a relevant doc counts as a "hit" even if it's a different document.         |
| 8   | **Can Recall@K be 1.0 while the RAG system still fails? Explain.**                              | Yes. Perfect recall means all relevant docs were retrieved, but if the LLM generator is unfaithful (hallucination), irrelevant to the question, or if the docs are retrieved but not used properly, the final answer can still be wrong.                                 |
| 9   | **How would you use Recall@K to detect gaps in your knowledge base?**                           | Run Recall@K evaluation across diverse queries. Queries with consistently low recall indicate missing content. Analyze what relevant documents are "missing" (judged by LLM) to identify knowledge gaps to fill.                                                         |
| 10  | **Why does increasing the number of retrieved documents not always improve Recall@K linearly?** | After retrieving the most relevant docs (high-recall region), additional retrieval brings increasingly irrelevant docs. The recall curve flattens because fewer remaining un-retrieved docs are actually relevant.                                                       |

### 🎭 10 Scenario-Based Questions

| #   | Scenario                                                                                               | Question & Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **RAG for drug interactions: Ground truth has 8 relevant docs. System retrieves 6 of them in top-10.** | **Q:** Calculate Recall@10 and what's the clinical impact? **A:** R@10 = 6/8 = 0.75. 25% of drug interactions missed — clinically dangerous. A patient could have an unreported dangerous combination. Must increase K or improve retriever.                                                                    |
| 2   | **After switching from TF-IDF to dense vector retrieval, Recall@5 drops from 0.80 to 0.60.**           | **Q:** Why might this happen and how to fix it? **A:** Dense retrieval misses exact keyword matches that TF-IDF caught. Fix: use hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense) with reciprocal rank fusion. Dense retrieval excels on semantic queries but can miss exact term matches.                                       |
| 3   | **Q&A system: Recall@K = 0.90 but users still complain answers are incomplete.**                       | **Q:** What else might be wrong if recall is high? **A:** High recall means relevant docs are retrieved, but the LLM might ignore parts of the context, truncate relevant passages, or the context window might be too full for the LLM to process all retrieved information effectively.                       |
| 4   | **Enterprise KB: Recall@10 for HR policy queries = 0.50. You have 200 HR documents.**                  | **Q:** How would you systematically improve recall? **A:** (1) Add metadata tagging to HR docs (department, policy type), (2) implement hierarchical retrieval (first retrieve HR category, then specific docs), (3) use query expansion with HR terminology synonyms.                                          |
| 5   | **You have Recall@5 = 0.70 and Recall@10 = 0.71. Adding more documents barely helps.**                 | **Q:** What does this flat recall curve tell you? **A:** The relevant docs are already mostly retrieved by K=5. Increasing K gives diminishing returns. The bottleneck is either (a) relevant docs genuinely don't exist, or (b) retriever ranking is good but embedding quality limits finding the last 30%.   |
| 6   | **Chatbot for technical manuals: Some queries have R@10=0.95, others have R@10=0.30.**                 | **Q:** How would you diagnose the low-recall queries? **A:** Analyze low-recall queries: are they using jargon not in documents? Are the relevant docs in a different format (images, tables)? Are the queries ambiguous? Use these insights to improve preprocessing, indexing, or chunking strategy.          |
| 7   | **Legal RAG: You want Recall@K ≥ 0.90 for all queries. Currently at 0.72.**                            | **Q:** What strategies would you use to close this gap? **A:** (1) Increase K, (2) query expansion using LLM to generate multiple query variations, (3) add hypothetical document embedding (HyDE), (4) multi-hop retrieval for complex queries, (5) fine-tune embedding model on legal domain.                 |
| 8   | **Product team wants to know: should we optimize for precision or recall in our shopping assistant?**  | **Q:** How would you recommend balancing the tradeoff? **A:** For e-commerce: optimize recall first (show all relevant products) then use reranking for precision (show most relevant at top). Missing a product the user wants hurts conversion. Showing some irrelevant products is a lesser problem.         |
| 9   | **Recall@K = 0.90 in offline evaluation but only 0.60 in A/B production test.**                        | **Q:** What might cause this 30% drop in production? **A:** (1) Production queries differ from test set, (2) new documents added post-evaluation, (3) embedding model drift, (4) query preprocessing differences. Solution: continuously evaluate on fresh production query samples.                            |
| 10  | **Multi-language RAG: English queries have Recall@10 = 0.85, Spanish queries = 0.50.**                 | **Q:** What's the root cause and how do you fix it? **A:** Embedding model performs better on English due to training data imbalance. Fix: use multilingual embedding model (mE5, multilingual-MiniLM), add language detection + language-specific retrieval, or translate queries to English before retrieval. |

sections.title: MRR — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
sections.body:
### 🧠 10 Conceptual Questions

| #   | Question                                                                                           | Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **What does MRR measure that Precision@K and Recall@K don't capture?**                             | MRR specifically captures the RANKING QUALITY of the retriever — is the FIRST relevant document placed near the top? P@K and R@K don't distinguish between finding a relevant doc at rank 1 vs rank K. MRR rewards higher-ranked first relevant docs.                                                    |
| 2   | **Why does MRR use reciprocal rank (1/rank) instead of linear decay (1 - rank/K)?**                | Reciprocal rank has a sharp penalty for first few positions. RR=1/1=1.0 vs RR=1/2=0.5 vs RR=1/3=0.33 — finding the answer at rank 2 instead of rank 1 is penalized heavily. Linear decay would be more forgiving, not capturing the user's experience accurately.                                        |
| 3   | **In what use cases is MRR the most appropriate metric to use?**                                   | MRR is ideal when: (1) there's typically ONE correct answer per query (Q&A systems), (2) users care most about the top result (voice assistants), (3) your RAG uses only the top-1 retrieved document for generation.                                                                                    |
| 4   | **What is the limitation of MRR in systems with multiple relevant documents?**                     | MRR only considers the FIRST relevant document. It ignores all other relevant docs at lower positions. For multi-document RAG where multiple chunks are passed to the LLM, NDCG is more appropriate as it considers all positions.                                                                       |
| 5   | **How does MRR change if you set a cutoff (MRR@K)?**                                               | MRR@K only counts a query as a "hit" if the first relevant doc appears within top-K. If relevant doc is at rank K+1, it contributes 0 to MRR. This better models the practical constraint of only showing K results.                                                                                     |
| 6   | **What MRR score would indicate an excellent RAG retriever? What would indicate a poor one?**      | MRR > 0.9 = Excellent (relevant doc almost always at rank 1). MRR 0.7-0.9 = Good. MRR 0.5-0.7 = Fair (relevant doc often at rank 2-3). MRR < 0.5 = Poor (relevant doc rarely at top).                                                                                                                    |
| 7   | **Can two systems have the same MRR but very different user experiences? Explain.**                | Yes. System A: All queries return relevant doc at rank 2 (MRR = 0.5). System B: Half queries return relevant doc at rank 1 (RR=1.0), half never find it (RR=0). Both have MRR=0.5. System A gives consistent mediocre experience; System B gives great experience for half, terrible for the other half. |
| 8   | **How would you improve MRR in a RAG system where relevant documents tend to appear at rank 3-4?** | (1) Use a reranker model to reorder retrieved docs, (2) improve query encoding (fine-tune on domain), (3) use HyDE or query expansion to better match document embeddings, (4) add BM25 to boost exact keyword matches to higher ranks.                                                                  |
| 9   | **Explain the relationship between MRR and user satisfaction in information retrieval systems.**   | Studies show user satisfaction drops significantly for rank 1 → rank 3. MRR captures this well because 1/1=1.0 vs 1/3=0.33 (a 67% drop). MRR correlates with "time to first relevant result" which directly predicts user satisfaction.                                                                  |
| 10  | **How is MRR used in the RAGAS framework specifically?**                                           | In RAGAS, MRR isn't a direct metric, but it influences Context Precision (how well the most relevant chunks are ranked at the top). A good RAGAS evaluation includes checking MRR separately to understand if the retriever is ranking quality correctly.                                                |

### 🎭 10 Scenario-Based Questions

| #   | Scenario                                                                                                | Question & Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Voice assistant: "Hey, what's the boiling point of water?" Relevant doc appears at rank 3.**          | **Q:** Calculate RR and explain user impact. **A:** RR = 1/3 = 0.33. For a voice assistant, this is terrible — only top-1 doc is used. User gets wrong/incomplete answer. Must achieve rank 1 for all simple factual queries.                                                                                                                                         |
| 2   | **After adding query expansion, MRR improves from 0.55 to 0.78. What does this mean practically?**      | **Q:** Explain what changed in the retrieval process. **A:** Average rank of first relevant doc improved significantly. If relevant doc was typically at rank 2-3 before, it's now at rank 1-2. Users will find answers faster. MRR gain of 0.23 = very significant improvement.                                                                                      |
| 3   | **Legal chatbot: MRR = 0.90 for statute queries but 0.45 for case law queries.**                        | **Q:** How would you diagnose and fix the case law problem? **A:** Case law has inconsistent structure and terminology. Fix: fine-tune embeddings on legal case documents specifically, add citation parsing, implement a case-law-specific chunking strategy (by case section), use metadata filters (jurisdiction, year).                                           |
| 4   | **RAG Q&A system serves 1000 daily queries. MRR = 0.65. How many users get relevant docs at rank 1?**   | **Q:** Estimate this and explain business impact. **A:** MRR 0.65 suggests ~65% of queries get relevant doc at rank 1 (roughly). 35% of 1000 = 350 users/day getting suboptimal answers. At scale, this significantly impacts user trust and repeat usage.                                                                                                            |
| 5   | **Two retrieval strategies: Dense (MRR=0.72) vs. Hybrid BM25+Dense (MRR=0.84). Production uses Dense.** | **Q:** Would you recommend switching? What factors to consider? **A:** Yes, 0.12 MRR improvement is substantial. Consider: latency increase from BM25 (usually <20ms additional), infrastructure complexity, and whether improvement holds across all query types. Run A/B test on 10% traffic first.                                                                 |
| 6   | **Student learning platform: MRR drops 30% for topics added recently vs. older topics.**                | **Q:** Why might new topics have lower MRR? **A:** New topic documents may have lower-quality embeddings (not enough similar training examples), inconsistent writing style, or insufficient documents. Solution: create more varied example documents for new topics, re-embed after 2-4 weeks of organic queries.                                                   |
| 7   | **Customer wants to know: "Why does the chatbot give wrong first answers 30% of the time?"**            | **Q:** How would you use MRR to explain this and propose a fix? **A:** MRR = 0.70 implies ~30% of queries don't get the relevant doc at rank 1. Explain: the retriever ranks relevant docs at position 2-3 for 30% of queries. Fix: add reranker model to rescore top-5 docs, should boost MRR to 0.85+.                                                              |
| 8   | **Medical RAG: MRR for drug dosage queries = 0.92, but for drug interaction queries = 0.51.**           | **Q:** What structural difference causes this gap? **A:** Dosage queries are simple (one document, specific fact). Interaction queries require multi-document reasoning. The interaction information may be spread across multiple documents, making single-doc retrieval insufficient. Use multi-hop retrieval and graph-based knowledge retrieval for interactions. |
| 9   | **You want to move from K=10 to K=5 retrieval to reduce LLM costs. MRR@5 vs MRR@10 differ by 0.15.**    | **Q:** Is reducing K a good tradeoff? What approach would you take? **A:** 0.15 MRR drop = significant quality loss. Before reducing K blindly: (1) Use a reranker to improve top-5 quality, (2) implement adaptive K (use K=3 for high-confidence queries, K=7 for uncertain ones), (3) check if MRR@5 is still above 0.7 for acceptable user experience.            |
| 10  | **After fine-tuning embedding model on domain data, MRR improves from 0.61 to 0.88 on test set.**       | **Q:** Should you immediately deploy this? What concerns exist? **A:** Not immediately. Concerns: (1) Overfitting to test set — evaluate on held-out queries, (2) catastrophic forgetting — check if MRR drops on general queries, (3) re-embed all documents (expensive), (4) A/B test in production before full rollout.                                            |

sections.title: NDCG — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
sections.body:
### 🧠 10 Conceptual Questions

| #   | Question                                                                                                               | Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **What key advantage does NDCG have over MRR and Precision@K?**                                                        | NDCG supports GRADED relevance (0, 1, 2, 3 scores) and considers ALL retrieved positions, not just the first relevant one. It rewards placing highly relevant docs at top positions more than slightly relevant ones.                                                        |
| 2   | **Explain why NDCG uses a logarithmic discount instead of a linear one.**                                              | Logarithmic discount (1/log₂(rank+1)) mimics human attention: the difference between rank 1 and rank 2 matters more than between rank 9 and rank 10. Users are much more likely to look at rank 1 than rank 3, but barely distinguish between rank 9 and 10.                 |
| 3   | **What is IDCG and why is it necessary for computing NDCG?**                                                           | IDCG (Ideal DCG) is the maximum possible DCG — the DCG you'd get if all retrieved documents were perfectly ranked by relevance (highest relevance at rank 1). Normalizing by IDCG makes NDCG comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant docs.              |
| 4   | **When would NDCG and MRR give different rankings of retrieval systems?**                                              | When relevant documents have varying relevance grades. System A: puts highly relevant doc at rank 2, NDCG rewards this well. System B: puts slightly relevant doc at rank 1. MRR gives System B better score (rank 1), but NDCG gives System A better score (grade matters). |
| 5   | **How do you assign relevance grades (0, 1, 2, 3) in practice for a RAG evaluation dataset?**                          | Use annotators to judge: 0 = Not relevant, 1 = Marginally relevant (mentions topic), 2 = Relevant (answers part of query), 3 = Highly relevant (completely answers query). Use LLM-as-Judge with a structured rubric to automate grading at scale.                           |
| 6   | **What is the interpretation of NDCG@K = 1.0 vs NDCG@K = 0.0?**                                                        | NDCG=1.0 = Perfect ranking — most relevant docs at top positions, exactly as ideal. NDCG=0.0 = No relevant documents retrieved OR worst possible ordering (most relevant at last position with 0 DCG).                                                                       |
| 7   | **How does NDCG@K change as K increases? What happens at very large K?**                                               | As K increases, more docs are considered. NDCG tends to increase initially then plateau as lower-ranked relevant docs add diminishing discounted gains. At very large K approaching all docs, NDCG → 1 if all relevant docs are eventually retrieved (just poorly ranked).   |
| 8   | **In a RAG context with K=5 retrieved chunks, explain how you would use NDCG to select between two embedding models.** | Annotate a diverse test set with relevance grades (0-3) for each query-document pair. Compute NDCG@5 for both models across all test queries. Average NDCG@5 directly tells you which model ranks relevant chunks higher. Higher NDCG = better context quality fed to LLM.   |
| 9   | **What is the difference between NDCG and MAP (Mean Average Precision)?**                                              | MAP assumes binary relevance (relevant/not relevant) and averages precision at each relevant document position. NDCG supports graded relevance and discounts lower positions logarithmically. NDCG is more informative when relevance degrees vary significantly.            |
| 10  | **How would you use NDCG to evaluate a reranker model separately from the initial retriever?**                         | Evaluate initial retriever: NDCG@K on retrieved docs. Then rerank and compute NDCG@K on the same set. If NDCG improves post-reranking, the reranker is effective. If NDCG doesn't improve, the reranker isn't capturing relevance grades correctly.                          |

### 🎭 10 Scenario-Based Questions

| #   | Scenario                                                                                                | Question & Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Job recommendation: Highly relevant job (grade=3) placed at rank 5, moderate (grade=2) at rank 1.**   | **Q:** How does this poor ranking affect NDCG and user experience? **A:** NDCG penalizes this heavily. A grade=3 doc at rank 5 contributes 3/log₂(6)=1.16, vs. 3/log₂(2)=3.0 at rank 1. The user sees a mediocre match first and may not scroll to the perfect match at rank 5.                                                                                     |
| 2   | **Your retrieval system NDCG@5 = 0.72. A reranker improves it to 0.89. Business impact?**               | **Q:** Quantify what this means for RAG quality. **A:** 24% improvement in ranking quality. In practice: more relevant context chunks appear first in LLM input, LLM generates better answers. If LLM uses top-2 chunks most, 0.89 NDCG means those top-2 are almost always highly relevant.                                                                        |
| 3   | **Academic paper search: NDCG@10 = 0.65. Analysis shows highly relevant papers cluster at rank 7-10.**  | **Q:** What specific fix would you recommend? **A:** The retriever ranks by similarity but not by relevance grade. Add a cross-encoder reranker that scores relevance more accurately. Alternatively, use citation count as a boost factor to surface more authoritative papers.                                                                                    |
| 4   | **Two retrieval models: Model A NDCG@5=0.80, Model B NDCG@5=0.78. Model A is 3x slower.**               | **Q:** Which would you choose for production RAG? **A:** Depends on latency SLA. If 3x slower means 300ms → 900ms latency, users notice. Consider: (1) Use Model B (faster) for initial retrieval, (2) Use Model A (better NDCG) as reranker on top-20 from Model B. Best of both worlds.                                                                           |
| 5   | **E-learning RAG: NDCG@5 = 0.85 for beginner queries, 0.52 for advanced queries.**                      | **Q:** What's the root cause of this disparity? **A:** Advanced queries use specialized terminology that embeddings don't capture well. Advanced content may be less represented in training data. Fix: fine-tune embeddings on advanced content, add difficulty metadata filter, use knowledge-graph enhanced retrieval for technical concepts.                    |
| 6   | **You need to create a 500-query evaluation dataset to compute NDCG. How would you do it efficiently?** | **Q:** Describe a practical annotation pipeline. **A:** (1) Sample 500 diverse production queries, (2) for each query, retrieve top-20 docs, (3) use GPT-4 to grade each doc 0-3 with rubric, (4) human spot-check 10% for quality, (5) compute NDCG@5 and @10. Iterate quarterly on fresh samples.                                                                 |
| 7   | **NDCG@K drops from 0.85 to 0.60 when you add a new 100K document corpus to your RAG KB.**              | **Q:** Why and how would you recover? **A:** New documents may have different embedding distributions, creating "false neighbors" that push relevant docs down. Fix: normalize embeddings, use HNSW index with tuned parameters, add metadata quality scores, consider separate indices for different document sources with fusion retrieval.                       |
| 8   | **Medical RAG: Annotators disagree 40% on relevance grades. NDCG annotation is unreliable.**            | **Q:** How do you address high annotator disagreement? **A:** Create detailed annotation guidelines with worked examples. Use 3-tier consensus (if 2/3 agree, use that grade; else adjudicate). Consider binary relevance instead of 4-level if graded annotation is too subjective. Use medical expert reviewers for ambiguous cases.                              |
| 9   | **Product manager asks: "Is NDCG@10 = 0.77 good or bad for our RAG chatbot?"**                          | **Q:** How would you frame this for a non-technical stakeholder? **A:** "Our chatbot ranks the most relevant information in the top 3 results about 77% of the way to perfect. This means users get high-quality answers 77% of the time. Industry benchmark for search is typically 0.70-0.85, so we're in a good range but have room to improve to 0.85+."        |
| 10  | **After 6 months in production, NDCG drifts down from 0.82 to 0.68 without any code changes.**          | **Q:** What causes evaluation metric drift and how do you detect/prevent it?\*\* **A:** Causes: (1) Semantic drift — users ask new types of questions, (2) Knowledge base staleness — relevant docs outdated, (3) Embedding model drift if cloud API updated. Prevention: monthly automated NDCG evaluation on sampled production queries, alerting if drops >0.05. |

sections.title: FAITHFULNESS — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
sections.body:
### 🧠 10 Conceptual Questions

| #   | Question                                                                                | Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **What is the difference between faithfulness and factual correctness in RAG?**         | Faithfulness measures if the answer is grounded in the retrieved context. Factual correctness measures if the answer is true in the real world. An answer can be faithful but wrong (if context is outdated/wrong) or correct but unfaithful (if LLM uses its parametric knowledge).                                 |
| 2   | **Why is faithfulness especially critical in enterprise RAG vs. general LLM chatbots?** | Enterprise RAG is explicitly designed to answer from company-specific documents. If the LLM goes beyond the context (even correctly), it violates the system's promise of grounded answers. Users can't distinguish faithful from unfaithful answers, eroding trust in the system.                                   |
| 3   | **How does the RAGAS framework measure faithfulness technically?**                      | RAGAS uses an LLM to: (1) extract atomic claims from the generated answer, (2) verify each claim against the retrieved context using NLI or LLM judgment, (3) faithfulness = supported_claims / total_claims. Each claim is treated as a binary hypothesis.                                                          |
| 4   | **What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic hallucination?**               | Intrinsic: generated content directly contradicts the source context (e.g., context says "1899", answer says "1891"). Extrinsic: generated content adds information not present in context (cannot be verified from source). Both reduce faithfulness but have different root causes.                                |
| 5   | **What prompt engineering techniques can improve faithfulness in RAG?**                 | (1) Explicit grounding instruction: "Answer ONLY from the provided context. Do not use outside knowledge", (2) Chain-of-thought with citation: "For each claim, cite which context passage it comes from", (3) Confidence prompting: "If the answer is not in context, say 'I don't know'".                          |
| 6   | **How would you detect faithfulness issues in a production RAG system at scale?**       | (1) Automated: use NLI model to check each answer claim against context, (2) Sampling: LLM-as-Judge evaluates 1-5% of daily outputs, (3) User feedback: thumbs down rate as proxy, (4) Semantic similarity between answer and context, (5) Named entity extraction comparison.                                       |
| 7   | **Can a RAG system have high faithfulness but still give poor user experience?**        | Yes. If the context itself is incomplete or irrelevant (low context recall/precision), the answer may be perfectly faithful to poor context. "Faithful garbage in, faithful garbage out." A system that says "I don't know" because context lacks info is technically faithful but frustrating.                      |
| 8   | **Why might a larger, more capable LLM produce lower faithfulness scores?**             | Larger LLMs have stronger parametric knowledge. When context is ambiguous or incomplete, they "fill in" from their training data — generating plausible but unfaithful content. Smaller models are more conservative and stick closer to context. Fine-tuning for faithfulness or using strict system prompts helps. |
| 9   | **How does temperature setting affect faithfulness in RAG?**                            | Higher temperature = more creative/diverse outputs = higher chance of straying from context = lower faithfulness. For RAG, use temperature 0 or close to 0 to make the model deterministic and context-bound. Temperature > 0.7 in RAG is usually harmful.                                                           |
| 10  | **What is self-consistency and how can it improve faithfulness detection?**             | Self-consistency generates multiple answers (different temperature/prompts) and finds the consensus. Claims appearing in most answers are likely grounded. Inconsistent claims across generations often indicate hallucination. Use majority voting on claims as a faithfulness signal.                              |

### 🎭 10 Scenario-Based Questions

| #   | Scenario                                                                                                       | Question & Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Insurance chatbot answers: "We cover flood damage." But context says "Flood requires separate $200 rider."** | **Q:** What type of hallucination is this and what's the severity? **A:** Intrinsic hallucination — directly contradicts context. Severity: CRITICAL. Customer could make financial decisions based on false information, leading to denied claims, complaints, and legal liability. Immediate remediation required.                                                                                                                                |
| 2   | **Faithfulness score = 0.95 in testing but 0.72 in production. Identify likely causes.**                       | **Q:** What are 3 possible root causes? **A:** (1) Production queries require multi-hop reasoning across multiple docs, forcing LLM to interpolate, (2) Production context chunks are longer/noisier, overwhelming LLM's attention, (3) Edge-case queries where LLM's parametric knowledge "kicks in" more aggressively than on test set.                                                                                                           |
| 3   | **Medical RAG faithfulness = 0.88. Team says "12% hallucination is acceptable." How do you respond?**          | **Q:** Make the business case for improving faithfulness. **A:** 12% hallucination in medical = 1 in 8 answers contains potentially dangerous wrong information. If chatbot handles 10,000 daily queries, 1,200 hallucinated medical responses/day. Risk: patient harm, medical malpractice liability, regulatory violations. Even 0.97+ faithfulness may be insufficient for clinical use.                                                         |
| 4   | **RAG system for HR policies: Faithfulness = 0.70 for benefits questions, 0.95 for PTO questions.**            | **Q:** Why might benefit questions have lower faithfulness? **A:** Benefits are complex, multi-factor decisions (varies by location, employment level, tenure). LLM may generalize across complex policy conditions. PTO is simple and uniform. Fix: restructure benefits chunks to be more atomic, or implement policy type classification with specialized prompts.                                                                               |
| 5   | **You add few-shot examples to the RAG prompt and faithfulness drops from 0.85 to 0.75.**                      | **Q:** How can examples cause faithfulness to drop? **A:** Few-shot examples may demonstrate a style that includes information beyond context. LLM learns to "add helpful context" from examples, increasing hallucination. Fix: ensure all few-shot examples are strictly grounded in their context, or remove examples and use zero-shot with explicit faithfulness instruction.                                                                  |
| 6   | **Legal RAG: Faithfulness = 0.92 overall, but 100% of hallucinated claims involve dates and numbers.**         | **Q:** What targeted fix would you implement? **A:** Numbers/dates are high-risk for hallucination. Add a post-processing step: extract all numbers and dates from the answer, verify each exists in the context. If a number in the answer isn't in context, either replace with "not specified" or flag for human review.                                                                                                                         |
| 7   | **Your RAG system needs to pass an audit: "All answers must be 100% grounded in policy documents."**           | **Q:** How would you technically achieve and verify this? **A:** (1) Strict prompt: "Use ONLY the provided documents. If information is not there, say 'This is not covered in current policy documents.'", (2) Faithfulness score threshold: block any answer with faithfulness < 0.95, (3) Citation requirement: force LLM to cite specific policy document and section for each claim, (4) Monthly audit of 200 sampled Q&As by compliance team. |
| 8   | **After switching from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4, faithfulness drops from 0.88 to 0.79.**                               | **Q:** Why might a better model produce less faithful answers? **A:** GPT-4 has more extensive parametric knowledge and is more confident in using it. When context is incomplete, GPT-4 "helpfully" fills in information it knows. GPT-3.5 stays closer to context because its parametric knowledge is weaker. Fix: stronger grounding instructions in system prompt, or use constrained decoding.                                                 |
| 9   | **Customer complaint: "Your chatbot told me something completely different from your website."**               | **Q:** How would you investigate this faithfulness failure? **A:** (1) Retrieve the conversation log and matched context, (2) Run faithfulness evaluation on that specific Q&A, (3) Identify which claims were unsupported, (4) Check if context chunk was outdated/incorrect, (5) Determine if it was hallucination (LLM) or wrong context (retriever). (6) Fix source: update context or add faithfulness guardrails.                             |
| 10  | **Team proposes: "Let's just add a disclaimer saying answers may not be accurate."**                           | **Q:** Why is this insufficient and what should you do instead? **A:** Disclaimers don't solve the problem and can reduce user trust further. Users still act on wrong information. Instead: (1) Fix faithfulness to >0.90, (2) Implement confidence scoring, (3) For low-confidence answers, show source document links, (4) For high-stakes queries (medical, legal, financial), always require human review.                                     |

sections.title: RAGAS SCORE — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
sections.body:
### 🧠 10 Conceptual Questions

| #   | Question                                                                             | Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1   | **What are the 4 core metrics in RAGAS and what does each measure?**                 | (1) Faithfulness: Is answer grounded in context?, (2) Answer Relevancy: Does answer address the question?, (3) Context Precision: Are retrieved chunks relevant to the question?, (4) Context Recall: Does context contain all needed info? Together they cover both retrieval and generation quality. |
| 2   | **Why does RAGAS use harmonic mean to combine metrics rather than arithmetic mean?** | Harmonic mean penalizes extreme low scores heavily. If faithfulness = 0.0 (pure hallucination), harmonic mean → 0 regardless of other scores. With arithmetic mean, poor faithfulness could be "averaged out" by good other scores. RAGAS ensures all dimensions must be good.                         |
| 3   | **What makes RAGAS "reference-free" and why is this advantageous?**                  | RAGAS can evaluate faithfulness and answer relevancy without ground truth answers by using LLM to judge claims against context. This allows evaluation of open-domain queries where ground truth doesn't exist. Traditional metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) require reference answers.                           |
| 4   | **In RAGAS, which metrics require ground truth answers and which don't?**            | Requires ground truth: Context Recall (needs to know what facts should be in context). Doesn't require ground truth: Faithfulness (context is ground truth), Answer Relevancy (uses LLM to generate reference questions from the answer).                                                              |
| 5   | **How would you use RAGAS to identify the weakest component in your RAG pipeline?**  | Run RAGAS and compare individual metric scores: Low Context Precision + Context Recall = Retri                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

ever problem. Low Faithfulness = Generation/LLM problem. Low Answer Relevancy = Prompt engineering problem. This component-level diagnosis allows targeted fixes rather than guessing. |
| 6 | **What is the minimum acceptable RAGAS score for a production RAG system?** | Generally: RAGAS > 0.85 = Production ready, 0.70-0.85 = Acceptable with monitoring, 0.55-0.70 = Needs improvement before production, < 0.55 = Major redesign needed. However, thresholds vary by domain — medical/legal require 0.90+. |
| 7 | **How would you extend RAGAS for a multi-turn conversational RAG system?** | Add: (1) Context Continuity score (does context reference previous turns correctly?), (2) Answer Consistency (do answers stay consistent across the conversation?), (3) Coreference faithfulness (are pronouns/references correctly grounded?). Evaluate at conversation level, not just single-turn. |
| 8 | **What are the limitations of RAGAS as an evaluation framework?** | (1) LLM-based evaluation is expensive at scale, (2) Judge LLM has its own biases and inconsistencies, (3) Doesn't capture user satisfaction directly, (4) Doesn't evaluate response latency, (5) Context Recall requires ground truth, (6) May not generalize across all domains equally. |
| 9 | **How would you build a continuous RAGAS evaluation pipeline in production?** | (1) Sample 1-5% of daily queries, (2) Retrieve context and generate answers as normal, (3) Run RAGAS asynchronously (offline), (4) Store scores in time-series DB, (5) Alert if any metric drops >0.05 week-over-week, (6) Dashboard for engineering team, (7) Monthly deep-dive review. |
| 10 | **Can RAGAS score be gamed or artificially inflated? How would you detect this?** | Yes: (1) Retriever can return only short, highly specific chunks → high Context Precision but low recall, (2) Generator can return very short, literal answers → high Faithfulness but low Relevancy. Detection: check metric balance (all should be high together), also run human spot-checks on high-RAGAS samples. |

RAGAS=0.63.** | **Q:** What is the single most important fix? **A:** Context Recall = 0.40 is the critical bottleneck dragging RAGAS down. The retriever is finding very precise chunks but missing most relevant information. Fix: increase K, improve query expansion, or restructure chunking to |

| 5 | **How would you use RAGAS to identify the weakest component in your RAG pipeline?** | Run RAGAS and compare individual metric scores: Low Context Precision + Context Recall = **Retriever problem** (fix embedding model, chunking, indexing). Low Faithfulness = **Generator problem** (fix prompt, temperature, model). Low Answer Relevancy = **Prompt engineering problem** (fix instruction clarity). This diagnostic approach pinpoints exact pipeline failures. |
| 6 | **What is the RAGAS score range and what thresholds indicate production readiness?** | RAGAS score ranges 0.0 to 1.0. Thresholds: >0.85 = Excellent (production ready), 0.70-0.85 = Good (minor improvements needed), 0.55-0.70 = Fair (significant work required), <0.55 = Poor (major rework before deployment). These are general guidelines — critical domains (medical, legal) require >0.90. |
| 7 | **How does RAGAS handle multi-turn conversations vs. single-turn Q&A?** | RAGAS is designed for single-turn Q&A. For multi-turn, each turn must be evaluated independently with its own retrieved context. The conversation history adds complexity — prior context may influence answers, requiring the evaluator to consider accumulated context across turns. |
| 8 | **Can RAGAS be gamed (high score but poor real-world quality)? How?** | Yes.
